● I've worked through Codex's checklist. 12 of its 14 items are now finished and
  checked on the desk; the remaining two, CI and MSIX, can't be finished from
  here and are listed at the end. All three test suites pass (controlcheck 38,
  presetcheck, presetverify 70), and the engine is running on the new build.

  Verified on the desk:
  - Windows brightness driving unison: moving the laptop's brightness through
    Windows from 41 to 71 moved unison and the Dell to 71. That's correct,
    because your Dell's calibrated range is 0–100.
  - Calibration: "Calibrate again" moves the slider to 0 and each display to its
    lowest setting, whether unison is on or off.
  - Display preview: it stays beside the details at 2200 and 1100 px window
    widths and moves below them at 760 px. It's the same size at all three, so
    it no longer gets crushed.
  - Quick panel: no white border, sections fold, and summoning it from the
    command line runs the new animation without a crash. The animation switch
    and Windows' own "Animation effects" setting both turn it off.
  - CLI: every command answers correctly when run read-only or as a dry run, and
    your settings file was left untouched.

  Bugs found and fixed:
  - Calibration cancel: Cancel left every display at its lowest brightness with
    the slider on 0. It now puts back the unison level and each display's
    brightness, confirmed live (17/17/17, then 0, then back to 17/17/17).
  - Apply ordering: dispctrl apply checked every display before switching
    topology, so it rejected monitors that the switch would turn on. The
    topology switch now runs first, waits for Windows to settle, and then plans
    everything else. In a dry run, those monitors are marked as waiting on the
    topology switch instead of failing.
  - Error output: with --json, some errors were printed as plain text. They now
    come back in the same JSON format as every other result.

  New:
  - Monitor reconnect: with unison on, a monitor that's plugged back in is set
    to the current unison level. This hasn't been tried with a real unplug and
    replug.
  - MST and Thunderbolt: the display details now say "yes" when Windows says a
    display is tunnelled over USB4, Thunderbolt or USB-C, or when it shares a
    DisplayPort connector with another display (a hub or daisy chain). Windows
    doesn't report the order in a chain. Neither applies to your desk, so only
    the "no" case has run on your hardware.
  - Examples: three new files in examples/: a request, a layout, and a script
    that reapplies the layout on hot-plug. The docs, the checklist and CLAUDE.md
    are updated.

  Still open:
  - GitHub builds and releases have never actually run. They need a push and a
    v0.1.0-beta tag.
  - The Microsoft Store package builds but hasn't been installed, signed or
    certified. That needs your Partner Center identity and a signing
    certificate. I didn't install it here because it would run a second copy
    alongside your live engine.

  Your brightness changed from 41/31 to 17/17 during the session. I took it as
  your own change and put back whatever was there before each test. Nothing is
  committed.

  file over settings.json, which fails if another process has it open, and on
  the load side a sharing violation gets misread as corruption, causing a good
  file to be replaced with defaults. Now I'll work on fixing this race
  condition.

  Windows' raw 0–100 value directly instead of converting through the same
  unison logic as other displays. I'll fix it so the laptop follows unison like
  every other display, converting Windows values back through the calibrated

● All seven items are done and verified on the desk, and both test suites pass
  (controlcheck is at 45 checks). GitHub Actions is the only part not proven,
  because I can't run it on GitHub without pushing.

  Windows brightness with unison (the one you flagged as important). The Windows
  slider and brightness keys now stay inside the laptop panel's calibrated
  range, 25–78 on your desk, and every display stays in step with it. Before,
  the laptop panel was put at the raw level, so it ran 0–100 while the others
  stayed in their ranges. Tested live:
  - Windows at 10 → unison 0, laptop held at 25, Dell at 0.
  - Windows at 60 → unison 66, Dell at 66.
  - Windows at 95 → unison 100, laptop held at 78, Dell at 100.

  Simple mode. A new card at the top of the Quick panel page. The panel then
  shows only an "All displays" slider with the unison switch, and one slider per
  display, with no icons, headers or footer. I greyed out only the options
  simple mode ignores. Width, stay open, animation and which displays are shown
  still apply in simple mode, so they stay live.

  Quick panel layout.
  - Unison now has one brightness icon instead of three, and its on/off switch
    sits in the section header.
  - Section headers are text only.
  - Resolution, refresh rate, scale, orientation, input and the monitor's own
    controls use text labels in one column instead of icons.
  - Chevrons line up at the right edge in every section.

  Open and close animation. The panel now slides its whole height out from
  behind the taskbar in about 260 ms and sinks back in about 180 ms, the way
  Windows' flyouts do. I recorded both directions frame by frame. The old
  version flashed an empty grey box first, and lit tiles flickered grey on every
  opening.

  Autostart and launch speed.
  - Scheduled task: the engine now starts from a scheduled task
    (DispCtrl.Engine) with no sign-in delay and at normal priority, instead of
    the Startup folder, which Windows holds back. This is already set up on your
    machine; the old shortcut and the stale Umbra.Engine task are removed.
  - Keep the quick panel ready (on by default): the first click now opens it in
    about 40 ms instead of about a second. The cost is a resident process of
    about 146 MB.
  - Open DispCtrl at sign-in: a new option, off by default.
  - Faster shipped builds: released builds are precompiled, so the CLI starts in
    about 180 ms instead of 234.
  - Not elevated: I kept the engine unelevated on purpose. Running it as admin
    would break the tray icon and stop the CLI and panel reaching it; the gamma
    limit still asks for admin itself.

  CLI. Monitor controls are no longer hardcoded. dispctrl display controls 
  --monitor 2 lists whatever the monitor reports, with readable keys:
  input-source, picture-mode, osd-language and so on. Then:
  - dispctrl display control --monitor 2 --name picture-mode --value games sets
    one control by its listed values.
  - display set --controls "contrast=70,input-source=hdmi-1" sets several at
    once.
  - Also new: display identify, display factory-reset --confirm, gamma get/set,
    and startup options (--preload-panel, --open-window).
  - Everything else the app saves was already reachable with settings set 
    --path.
  - docs/CLI.md has a table mapping app features to commands.

  Bugs found along the way:
  - Settings save crash: the app crashed at 07:03 while you were dragging the
    unison slider. Saving settings.json failed whenever another process was
    reading it. Worse, a failed read could move a perfectly good settings file
    aside and reset everything to defaults. Both are fixed and covered by tests.
  - Gamma limit: lifting the limit never reached the engine until it restarted.
  - Panel behind windows: the preloaded panel opened behind other windows; it
    now stays on top.
  - Identify hotkey: it never worked; it does now.

  GitHub Actions. Every push now builds, runs the tests, publishes, and packs
  the Microsoft Store MSIX. Tagged releases can also sign the MSIX if you add a
  certificate as the SIGNING_CERT_BASE64 and SIGNING_CERT_PASSWORD secrets. The
  workflows pass actionlint, and I ran the same build, publish and package steps
  locally without errors. They'll only be proven once you push.

  Two things aren't tested yet: bringing a monitor back into unison when it's
  plugged back in (no physical replug), and installing or certifying the MSIX
  (that needs your Store identity and a signing certificate).

  The desk is as I found it this session: brightness 50/50, unison 50, Dell
  contrast 75, night light off, simple mode off. Nothing is committed.

  Laptop taskbar, bottom half missing. Explorer had left the laptop's taskbar
  with a clipping region 48 px tall on a bar that's 96 px tall at 200%. Windows
  draws nothing outside a window's region, so the bottom half simply never
  appeared. My earlier repaint fix couldn't help because the pixels were
  clipped, not stale. I cleared the region and the bar now draws in full;
  Explorer didn't put it back. The engine now checks every second, and each time

  glass helper's build script. The helper's version is a hash of that script, so
  Explorer refused the rebuilt helper. I restored the script exactly and glass
  is attached again; there's now a note in CLAUDE.md warning about it.

  Windows brightness and unison. The laptop panel now stays inside its
  calibrated range (25–78 on your desk), and the other displays follow the
  Windows slider while you drag it. The choppiness had two causes: the Dell
  waited until you stopped dragging and then jumped, and the laptop was pulled
  back into range mid-drag, fighting the slider. The Dell now follows about
  every 90 ms during the drag, and the range correction waits until the slider
  has been still for 400 ms.

  One limit I can't remove: Windows' slider always shows the laptop's actual
  backlight level, so it can't also read 0–100 as the unison level. Dragging it
  below the floor snaps back to the floor once you let go.

  Quick panel.
  - Title bar: the "…" menu is gone; both things in it are already on the Quick
    panel page and the tray icon's right-click menu. The title bar is now
    density, lock, pin and settings.
  - Lock: stops the title dragging the panel and puts it back in its place. It's
    currently switched on in your settings, which I didn't do, so presumably
    you tried it.
  - Tile flyouts: Night light, Focus, OLED care, Keep awake, Unison and Dark
    mode now open full flyouts with sliders and switches, like the Taskbar tile.
    I opened the Night light one and checked it.
  - Removed tiles: Taskbar glass, Auto-hide and Transparency are gone, since the
    Taskbar tile's flyout already has all three.

  Device library. It replaces the old collect → view → submit steps.
  - History: every monitor this PC sees is recorded locally, with every code it
    lists and the values each was seen at. No serials are stored.
  - Mapping: dispctrl devices probe watches the codes nobody has named while you
    change settings in the monitor's own menu. devices map then names one for
    that model, for the whole brand, or for every monitor, and models can link
    to each other to share mappings.
  - Writing: a mapped manufacturer code can be written only if its mapping is
    marked writable.
  - Sharing: devices share opens one GitHub issue with the model's record and
    your mappings, after the same privacy scrub as before.
  - Backend: a GitHub workflow turns that issue into a pull request for review,
    and another validates every change to devices/.
  - App: a new Devices page does all of this through the same commands.
  - Tested: end to end on the Dell in a throwaway data folder, so your real data
    is untouched.

  CLI coverage. I went through every page, and docs/CLI-COVERAGE.md maps each
  control to its command. Filled gaps: hotkeys (hotkeys add --keys "Ctrl+Alt+Up"
  …), display reset, wallpaper fit, per-monitor unison limits, and opening the
  Windows settings pages. I also fixed three CLI bugs:
  - taskbar get returned unrelated settings, and taskbar set could change unison
    by name.
  - The CLI's unison command still pushed the laptop panel to 0–100.
  - display reset --factory was refused before it ran.

  Repo cleanup.
  - Notes moved out: the Codex session log, the session transcript and the
    prompt you gave the other agent are now in a git-ignored .notes/ folder,
    still on your disk.
  - Duplicate task registration: tools/DispCtrl.ps1 -Install now uses the same
    startup task as the app instead of registering its own slower one.
  - Checked: every tool builds, and two leftover old names are fixed.

  Desk: laptop 52, Dell 51, unison 51 (inside the calibrated mapping), night
  light off, simple mode off, no hotkeys. Nothing is committed.

  The design is written up in docs/DEVICE-LIBRARY.md.

● I found why the keys got stuck going up, fixed it, and rebuilt and restarted
  the engine. I couldn't press the laptop's brightness keys myself (a script
  can't send them), so please give them a try.

  What went wrong: your down presses all registered, reaching unison 0 with the
  laptop held at its calibrated floor of 25. The three up presses you made after
  that never registered. Two things were killing them:

  - The correction's own echo: when the engine pulls the laptop back to 25, that
    write raises a brightness event of its own. That event could land just
    after your key press and replace it, so the engine only ever saw "25", which
    is still unison 0, and nothing moved.
  - Correcting at the wrong moment: the floor correction compared the laptop
    with the saved unison level. A press that had already moved the panel to 35,
    but hadn't been read yet, looked out of place, so it was undone.

  The slider hid this because a drag sends a steady stream of values that
  outruns both problems, and it only ever showed up coming up from the floor.

  Fix: the engine now recognises its own write and ignores only that echo. It
  only corrects the laptop when it's genuinely outside its calibrated range, and
  it waits until nothing has happened for 400 ms. I replayed your sequence with
  presses timed to hit the race: 34 → unison 17, 54 → 55, 74 → 92, 84 → unison
  100, with the laptop at 78 and the Dell at 100. Everything was restored
  afterwards.

  The top is capped by your calibration. The laptop goes up to 78, the ceiling
  you set, and Windows' slider can't show more than that. If you want the laptop
  to reach 100% at unison 100, recalibrate and take the brightest point higher.

  If the keys still stop, the engine log (%LOCALAPPDATA%\DispCtrl\engine.log)
  now records every press it ignores and why. Send me those lines and I'll know
  exactly what your keys are sending.

● This is the same list as your previous message, and all of it went in last
  round. The running engine and the preloaded panel are both on that build. In
  case any of it hasn't shown up for you, here's where each one is:

  - Simple mode: there's no layout (density) button in the title bar, and the
    panel is only as tall as its sliders. It ignores "Fixed height" while simple
    mode is on.
  - OLED protection section: the on/off switch is in the section header.
    Underneath are dim to, after (minutes), fade, "dim further after longer",
    that second stage's "then after" and "down to" (greyed until the second
    stage is on), pause during fullscreen, and "rest every OLED display now".
    The OLED care tile's arrow opens the same rows.
  - Focus mode section: the switch is in the header too. Underneath is every
    option: dim others, wait, fade, the transition between windows, the seven
    switches, and a "never dim these apps" box.
  - Folded by default: OLED protection, Focus, Display mode, Taskbar and Night
    light start folded when added, and stay open once you open them. Your panel
    already had them folded, so it looks the same as before.
  - Indent: rows under an open section, or under a display, sit a little in from
    the header.
  - Per-display switches: they now stretch across the full width in equal
    columns, with space above and below.
  - Hotkeys:
    - The page offers 21 actions, up from 9, including focus, OLED care and
      rest, keep awake, dark mode, the taskbar, glass, contrast, identify and
      the quick panel.
    - Seven defaults are set up for you: Ctrl+Alt+Page Up / Page Down for
      unison, N night light, F focus, K keep awake, I identify, D the quick
      panel.
    - "Restore the defaults" on the page, or dispctrl hotkeys reset, brings them
      back.
    - Unison hotkeys now move the displays even when the app is closed.
  - Presets: save icon in the navigation.
  - Display preview in a narrow window: the picture now comes first, above the
    details, lined up on the same left edge, and the copy button sits on "The
    panel" line instead of its own row.

  see, and I'll look at that one specifically.

      17 +                                                               
      18 +## What is in scope                                            
      19 +                                                               
      20 +DispCtrl runs unelevated as the signed-in user, and it has some
         + surfaces that                                                 
      21 +matter:                                                        
      22 +                                                               
      23 +- **The engine's named-pipe command broker.** It is scoped to t
         +he current user and                                            
      24 +  session. Any way for another user, another session, or a lowe
         +r integrity level                                              
      25 +  to send it commands is in scope.                             
      26 +- **Monitor records.** `dispctrl contribute` and `devices share
         +` build text meant                                             
      27 +  for publication. Any way for a serial number, a device path o
         +r instance id, a                                               
      28 +  file path, or the account name to survive the scrub into that
         + text is a                                                     
      29 +  vulnerability, and treated as one. See the "Publishing device
         + records" section                                              
      30 +  of [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md).                                   
      31 +- **Settings and device-definition parsing.** `settings.json`, 
         +presets and                                                    
      32 +  device definitions are read from disk, and some come from oth
         +er people.                                                     
      33 +- **The elevated gamma-range write**, the only operation that a
         +sks for                                                        
      34 +  administrator rights.                                        
      35 +- **The installer and the release pipeline.**                  
      36 +                                                               
      37 +Physical access to the monitors and the DDC/CI bus is out of sc
         +ope, as is a                                                   
      38 +process already running as the same user.

● The release pipeline, README, MIT licence and packaging automation are
  written. The installer compiles and every workflow passes actionlint, but I
  haven't run the installer on your machine and nothing has run on GitHub yet. I
  haven't committed or pushed anything.

  How a release works now
  1. Push a tag like v0.2.0 (with a hyphen, such as v0.2.0-beta.1, it becomes a
     beta prerelease).
  2. release.yml builds and tests everything, signs it if you've added a
     certificate, and makes the installer .exe, the portable and CLI zips, and
     the Store MSIX with checksums.
  3. It opens a draft release whose notes come from that version's section of
     CHANGELOG.md, plus install instructions and checksums.
  4. When you publish the draft as a stable release, the new distribute.yml
     sends an update to winget and submits the MSIX to the Microsoft Store. The
     Store submission waits for approval in a GitHub environment first, because
     a submission can't be pulled back once certification starts.
  5. build.yml also builds the installer on every push, so a packaging break is
     caught by the commit that causes it.

  The installer installs for the current user only, with no admin rights, into
  %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\DispCtrl:
  - It registers the sign-in task, starts the engine, and can add a desktop
    shortcut and a PATH entry.
  - It always stops the engine gracefully before overwriting or uninstalling. If
    the engine won't stop, setup refuses rather than kill it and strand a
    taskbar.
  - Uninstalling keeps your settings.
  - My first draft removed the sign-in task unconditionally, which would have
    deleted your development build's task. It now removes the task only when it
    points into the installer's own folder. I checked that logic against your
    real task without changing it; the task and engine are still running.

  Other things added:
  - Project files: README, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, code of conduct, CHANGELOG,
    bug and feature issue forms, a PR template and dependabot. The existing
    device issue template still works.
  - Scripts: new build/Installer.ps1, build/Sign.ps1 and build/ReleaseNotes.ps1;
    Publish.ps1 and Package.ps1 gained a -Sign switch.
  - Signing scope: only DispCtrl's own binaries are signed. The taskbar-glass
    helper is left alone because its revision is pinned.
  - Version: DispCtrlVersion in Directory.Build.props wasn't used anywhere
    before. It is now the default build version, and a stable tag that doesn't
    match it fails the release.
  - Docs: docs/RELEASING.md is rewritten as the full procedure, and CLAUDE.md
    and the checklist carry the new traps.

  I checked the README against the code and corrected three things:
  - Ctrl+Alt+D opens the quick panel, not dark mode.
  - There is no sunset schedule for night light.
  - Presets are off in release builds, so they're described as in development.

  dispctrl diagnostics includes monitor serials and your account name, so the
  bug-report advice now says to review it before pasting.

  Not yet tested:
  - Installer: I compiled it from a real bundle (73 MB) using a portable Inno
    Setup, but didn't install it here because that would re-point your sign-in
    task. It needs a clean user account or a VM.
  - GitHub: no workflow has run there yet.
  - Store upload: that step follows Microsoft's documented flags but hasn't been
    used against a real Partner Center account.

  What you need to do:
  - To distribute: set the secrets and variables in the "One-time setup" table
    in docs/RELEASING.md. Each distribution job does nothing until its variable
    is set.
  - Before winget updates: the first winget submission has to be made by hand.
  - Before the Store: reserve the name in Partner Center.

  The desktop bundle is 281 MB, mostly WinUI language folders. Limiting it to
  English (SatelliteResourceLanguages) would shrink both the zip and the
  installer. That's a separate change, so I left it.

● There's now a one-command developer setup and build for Windows (build.cmd)
  and for Linux, macOS or WSL (build.sh). I ran both end to end: on this
  machine, and on a fresh copy in WSL Ubuntu. Nothing is committed.

  Windows: build.cmd
  - Double-click it for a menu, or run it with a command: build.cmd doctor,
    setup, build, test, run engine|app|panel|cli, publish, installer, package,
    release, clean, options.
  - setup checks for everything needed. It installs .NET 10 or MinGW only when
    you add -Install (via winget). It downloads Inno Setup as a portable copy
    into .tools/ and restores packages, which brings MakeAppx and signtool
    without a Windows SDK install. The paths it finds are saved in
    build/local.json, which git ignores.
  - build stops the engine gracefully, builds, and restarts the engine through
    its sign-in task.
  - release produces the zips, installer, MSIX and release notes locally, the
    same way the release workflow does.
  - Options: Debug or Release, beta or stable, a version number, and building
    without the native taskbar-glass helper (for machines without MinGW). These
    are saved between runs. -Sign and -NoRestart apply to one run only.

  Linux, macOS, WSL: build.sh
  - It builds everything except the WinUI window, whose XAML compiler only runs
    on Windows.
  - setup installs .NET into .tools/ with no sudo.
  - test runs presetverify and devicecheck. controlcheck and presetcheck call
    Windows display APIs, so they only run on Windows.

  What I ran
  - This machine:
    - doctor and setup found every tool.
    - build stopped the engine, rebuilt it, and restarted it through its task.
      The glass helper kept its revision, so Explorer is unaffected.
    - test passed all four checks.
    - The script also parses under Windows PowerShell 5.1.
  - WSL: setup, build and test all passed on a clean copy, using temporary
    folders I've since removed.
  - Bug fixed: the first build run left the engine stopped. The script read the
    engine's path after stopping it, when that path is no longer available. It
    now reads it first; I restarted your engine and it's running now.
  - Not exercised: setup -Install (the winget installs) and build.sh --native
    (building the glass helper on Linux).

  Other changes
  - DispCtrl.Engine.csproj:
    - A new SkipTaskbarGlass switch builds the engine without the native helper.
    - Off Windows, the helper step runs pwsh instead of powershell.exe. Under
      WSL, powershell.exe reached Windows' own MinGW with Linux paths and failed
      to link.
  - global.json pins the .NET 10 SDK.
  - .gitattributes keeps build.sh in Unix line endings on Windows checkouts,
    since bash can't run it otherwise.
  - .vscode/tasks.json makes VS Code's build and test tasks call the same
    scripts.
  - docs/DEVELOPING.md covers every command and option; the README,
    CONTRIBUTING, CLAUDE.md and the checklist now point to it.

  When you commit, run git add --chmod=+x build.sh so it stays executable on
  Linux.

           ue hdmi-1

          -up --step 5

          + --step 10

          +act to hotplug and changes

      112 -## Privacy                                                    
      208 +The one thing that can leave your machine is a monitor report,
          + and only when you                                            
      209 +send it. **Displays > Monitor library** or `dispctrl contribut
          +e` builds a record

          +rs, device paths,                                             
      211 +file paths, your account name and your current settings are re
          +moved. You see                                                
      212 +the exact text first. Sending it opens a prefilled GitHub issu
          +e in your own                                                 
      213 +browser, and you press Submit or you don't.

  exceed GitHub's listing limits. I'll restructure into

  the repo while shipping only definitions and a compact index with the app.

● I restructured devices/ so it will hold thousands of monitors, and builds now
  clear out old output and finish by printing where everything went. All checks
  pass and a full local release runs cleanly. Nothing is committed.

  New layout: one folder per manufacturer, one per model

  devices/
    CATALOG.md            every model, as a table per manufacturer   (generated)
    index.json            the same, one line per model, for tools    (generated)
    common.json           mappings for every monitor                 (optional)
    DEL/
      brand.json          mappings for every Dell                    (optional)
      A234/
        record.md         what the U2424H reports about itself
        definition.json   what its codes mean
    SDC/4154/record.md

  - Contributions can't clash. Each shared monitor adds only its own folder, so
    two pull requests never touch the same file. The catalogue and index are
    rebuilt automatically after each merge, so contributors never edit them.
  - The app stays fast. Before, it read every shipped definition file each time
    it looked up a monitor. Now it opens at most three files per monitor, found
    directly from the model key, and caches them.
  - Downloads stay small. Only definitions ship with the app. Full records stay
    in the repository; the one piece of code that read them turned out to be
    unused, and I removed it.
  - Validation is stricter. It now rejects files in the wrong place, badly named
    folders, and records containing a user path or device ID. I planted each of
    those and it caught them all.
  - Tested at scale: a made-up library of 3,000 models from 150 manufacturers
    validates in about 8 seconds, with an index of 276 KB.
  - Tooling: devicecheck migrate moved the existing Dell and Samsung files into
    the new layout, and a sample share lands in its own folder when processed.

  Builds
  - Old build files are removed automatically. Every build folder still held the
    old flat device files from earlier builds, including records that must not
    ship; each build now deletes them. .\build.cmd build -Rebuild gives a
    completely clean build.
  - Output paths are printed. build ends by listing where the app, engine and
    CLI are. release lists every file with its size. -Open also opens the folder
    in Explorer.
  - Releases go to one folder: artifacts\beta-0.1.0\, holding the zips,
    installer, MSIX, checksums and release notes. Earlier builds are cleared
    first unless you add -Keep. This run removed 1.9 GB of old builds, and the
    folder is now 777 MB for one complete release.

  Bug fixed along the way: release rebuilds into the folders your running engine
  uses, but it never stopped the engine, so on your machine it would have
  failed with a locked-file error. It now stops the engine gracefully and
  restarts it afterwards, which it did during this run.

  devices mapping themselves without clicks, the broken Share button, making
  every reset button work, and a donate button on the main page. I haven't
  touched those yet; say if you want them next.

  exits early, leaving everything but protection settings (unison slider, night
  light, display cards, quick panel) stale until restart. I'll fix both resets
  now.
